extracted.intended_audience: peer reviewers and journal editors evaluating submitted systematic reviews / manuscripts (especially on open peer review and scholarly publishing)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating a submitted systematic review manuscript (here: on open peer review) for scientific soundness, methodological transparency, appropriate analysis, clarity of presentation, and fit between claims and evidence. Reviewers are asked to assign an overall status and answer specific reproducibility and validity questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer decision / status
rubrics_metrics.description: Alongside their report, reviewers assign a status to the article: Approved; Approved with reservations; Not approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approved — The paper is scientifically sound in its current form and only minor, if any, improvements are suggested. Approved with reservations — A number of small changes, sometimes more significant revisions are required to address specific details and improve the paper's academic merit. Not approved — Fundamental flaws in the paper seriously undermine the findings and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale and objectives clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the rationale for, and objectives of, the Systematic Review clearly stated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduction should clearly state definitions and the scope/ethos (e.g., definition of 'open science' or 'open peer review') so the frame of the paper is clear and contested meanings are unpacked where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods reproducibility and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Are sufficient details of the methods and analysis provided to allow replication by others?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide complete search strategy (databases searched, search terms for each database, date ranges), inclusion/exclusion criteria, how records were identified/selected, PRISMA checklist or equivalent. Explicitly outline limitations of the search strategy and any discipline-specific choices (e.g., treatment of SSH literature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the statistical analysis and its interpretation appropriate?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If statistical methods are used, ensure they are appropriate to the data and transparently reported. If reviewer cannot assess quantitative methods, recommend consultation with a qualified statistician.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusions supported by results
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the conclusions drawn adequately supported by the results presented in the review?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusions should be proportional to the evidence presented; limitations and uncertainty should be acknowledged and any strong claims (e.g., about efficiency of interventions) justified by evidence. Highlight where evidence is lacking and avoid over-generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing interests disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Competing Interests: reviewers/authors must disclose relevant competing interests (e.g., employment, affiliations, prior work that may be cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State any competing interests clearly in the report (e.g., 'No competing interests were disclosed' or list the relationship). Transparency about potential conflicts is required for readers to evaluate possible bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer Expertise: disclose domain expertise and confirm that you have read the submission and have an appropriate level of expertise to assess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include institutional affiliation and relevant areas of expertise. Explicitly confirm: 'I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Define key terms and scope in Introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction should clearly define contested terms (e.g., 'open science', 'open peer review') and state the ethos/scope used in the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where terms are contested across disciplines, unpack tensions and state which operational definition the study uses so readers understand the analytic frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategy breadth and database reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Search strategy must report which databases/search engines were used (e.g., Web of Science, Google Scholar, JSTOR, disciplinary databases, Google, Google Books), and provide search terms for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only one database was used initially, justify enrichment strategies (citation chasing, web searches) and be explicit about how non-WoS literature (e.g., blogs, books) was included. Document numbers and selection process to support claims about comprehensiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of disciplinary differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Address differences between disciplines (e.g., STEM vs social sciences & humanities) in methods, interpretation, and implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how search/analysis accommodates SSH literature; include discipline-specific breakdowns of traits/findings (figures/tables) and discuss how disciplinary practices may affect definitions and evidence about open peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results presentation (figures and tables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use figures and tables to translate findings and ideas presented in the results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear visualizations (e.g., taxonomy breakdowns, trait distributions by discipline) and ensure figures are accurate and match stated counts; these help readers grasp patterns across the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish editorial selection from peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid conflating editorial selection/decision-making with the technical process of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about which problems/solutions relate to peer review (vetting, technical checking, substantive feedback) versus editorial processes (acceptance/selection, editorial policies, publication delays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion: engage relevant literature and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion should engage with relevant prior work (including disciplinary sources and influential critiques) and consider whether innovations (e.g., open participation, mentorship, platform decoupling, real-time review) change the role/purpose of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and engage with key works (e.g., Fitzpatrick, discipline-specific white papers) where appropriate; explicitly discuss implications (mentorship, interactions between reviewers, platform effects) and whether questions lie in- or out-of-scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title and claims must match methods (systematic vs non-systematic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the paper's title and claims (e.g., calling the work a 'systematic review') reflect the actual methods used and their rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the search/enrichment process is not strictly systematic, adjust the title or clearly state methodological limits so readers are not misled about comprehensiveness or replicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and internal consistency of taxonomy/figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxonomies, counts, and figures must be internally consistent and accurately reported (e.g., verify number of definitions, correct duplicated rows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-check labels, totals and figure legends; correct obvious errors (duplicated entries, miscounts) and document corrections in revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitly state limitations and suggested future work
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions should include explicit limitations of the study and identify areas for future research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight methodological limits (e.g., scope exclusions such as literature not mentioning 'open peer review' explicitly), disciplinary blind spots, and where evidence is insufficient; recommend concrete next steps or guideline clarifications where appropriate.
